title: About
text:
I’m a social and behavioral science researcher. I have a PhD in social psychology from New York University. I use a multimethod approach to understand the interrelation between public attitudes and policy.
Tools: R · Stata · Mplus · SPSS
Methods: regression & panel models · causal inference · SEM / CFA · latent class & growth models · survey data · qualitative coding

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
NoteAt a glance





Question

What do people think causes poverty, and how do these beliefs relate to welfare and labor policies?

Data

Survey responses fielded in 13 countries (N = 6,500 with representative samples) integrated with country-level labor and welfare policies

Methods

Multi-national survey study with three-level mixed-effects regression

Findings

Reduced government spending predicts greater endorsement of individualist and fatalist attributions, and labor deregulation predicts greater endorsement of individualist attributions.

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
Background
Despite an abundance of economic wealth in the 21st century, poverty remains one of the challenges facing societies worldwide. Social scientists have long contended that the reasons people give for why poverty exists are related to their preferences for different policies. Little work, however, has looked at the relationship between actual policies and poverty beliefs. Our study examines three types of poverty attributions people give for why some people are poor: individualist (e.g., poor people are lazy), structural (e.g., the system is corrupt), and fatalist (e.g., poor people are unlucky). We study 13 countries, including commonly studied Western societies (e.g., the United States and the United Kingdom) and underrepresented societies (e.g., Egypt and Saudi Arabia).

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
Attributions across countries
Before modeling, we compared mean endorsement of each attribution type by country. Countries are ordered from least to most market-oriented, using the average of their government size and labor regulation scores.






Figure 1: Mean endorsement of structural, individualist and fatalist attributions by country (95% CI). Countries are ordered by the average of government size and labor regulation.



The R code below reshapes the survey data to long format (one row per respondent × attribution type), computes country means with 95% confidence intervals, and draws the plot.


Show R code

library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(reshape2)

df1 <- read_dta("Goudarzi&Napier_2025_full.dta")

# Long format: one row per respondent x attribution type
df_att_poverty <- subset(df1, select = c("country", "respondent_serial",
                                         "ind4", "struct4", "fate3",
                                         "gov_size", "labor_reg"))
df_att_poverty_long <- melt(df_att_poverty,
                            id = c("country", "respondent_serial",
                                   "gov_size", "labor_reg"))
colnames(df_att_poverty_long)[colnames(df_att_poverty_long) == "variable"] <- "att_type"
df_att_poverty_filtered <- df_att_poverty_long %>% filter(!is.na(value))

# Country means with 95% confidence intervals
summary_data <- df_att_poverty_filtered %>%
  group_by(country, att_type) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_value = mean(value),
    ci_lower   = mean_value - qt(0.975, n()) * sd(value) / sqrt(n()),
    ci_upper   = mean_value + qt(0.975, n()) * sd(value) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Order countries by the average of government size and labor regulation
order <- c("Sweden", "Brazil", "Japan", "South Korea", "Turkey", "UK", "Indonesia",
           "Hungary", "Russia", "US", "India", "Egypt", "Saudi Arabia")
country_mapping <- c("Brazil", "Egypt", "Hungary", "India", "Indonesia", "Japan",
                     "Russia", "Saudi Arabia", "South Korea", "Sweden", "Turkey",
                     "UK", "US")
summary_data$country  <- factor(country_mapping[summary_data$country], levels = order)
summary_data$att_type <- factor(summary_data$att_type,
                                levels = c("struct4", "ind4", "fate3"))

# Plot
figure1 <- ggplot(summary_data,
                  aes(x = country, y = mean_value, color = att_type,
                      group = interaction(country, att_type))) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper), width = 0.1,
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Mean Value", color = "Attribution Type") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "#4CAF50"),
                     labels = c("Structural", "Individualist", "Fatalist")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 5)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

ggsave("figure1_lineplot.png", plot = figure1,
       width = 10, height = 7, units = "in", dpi = 300)

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
Data and model
We fit a three-level mixed-effects regression, with attribution types (level 1) nested in respondents (level 2), nested in countries (level 3). The outcome is attribution endorsement. The model was estimated in two steps.
Step 1: Individual-level predictors

Attribution type: dummy codes for individualist and fatalist (structural = reference)
Subjective socioeconomic status (SES), centered within country
Attribution type × SES

Step 2: Economic policies

Small government
Labor deregulation
Attribution type × small government
Attribution type × labor deregulation

Controls (both steps)

Individual level: gender, age, college education, income
Country level: SES (centered between countries), Gini, DI, HDI

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
Results
The figures below show predicted endorsement of each attribution type in countries 1 SD below and 1 SD above the mean on each policy measure, from the Step 2 model.









Figure 2: Small government











Figure 3: Labor deregulation






Predicted attribution endorsement at low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD) levels of small government and labor deregulation (95% CI).

title: Cross-National Study of Poverty Attributions and Economic Policies
text:
Takeaways


Structural attributions are the most strongly endorsed in most of the 13 countries, but the gap between attribution types varies widely across countries and is related to small government and labor laws.
In countries with smaller governments, people more strongly endorse individualist and fatalist explanations for poverty.
In countries with more deregulated labor markets, people more strongly endorse individualist explanations.


Full code: goudarzi-napier-2026-plots.R
Paper: Goudarzi, S., & Napier, J. L. (2026). The association between neoliberal policies and attributions of poverty in 13 countries. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 17(4), 480–491.

title: Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
text:
NoteAt a glance





Question

Is there a dynamic relationship between beliefs about income inequality at the individual level and economic policies at the societal level?

Data

Economic policies derived from official statistics, legal data, and expert surveys


Attitudes toward income inequality were measured in the World Values Survey

Analysis

Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling to analyze longitudinal relationships between neoliberal structures and individuals’ preferences for income (in)equality in more than 160 countries over 5 waves.

Findings

Market-oriented economic policies predicted higher preference for income inequality a few years later.

title: Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
text:
Background
Neoliberalism refers to free market policies of reduced welfare spending, privatization, and deregulation of labor markets. One reason advocates argue for enacting these policies is that they reward hard work, rather than free riding. In this project, we examined how variations in market-oriented policies relate to beliefs about income inequality in more than 160 countries over more than two decades.

title: Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
text:
Data
Free Market Economic policies data: Composite of items from Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom Index (EFI), such as government consumption, transfers and subsidies, top marginal income and payroll tax, hiring and firing regulation, centralized collective bargaining.
Attitudes towards income inequality survey measure from WVS with answers ranging from “Incomes should be made more equal” (1) to “There should be greater incentives for individual effort” (10)
Analysis was conducted on five waves of data, from WVS Waves 3 (1995–1998) through 7 (2017–2019).

title: Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
text:
Results
As shown in Table 1, Lag-1 neoliberalism predicted higher preference for income inequality at time t (φ4i), whereas Lag-1 preference for income inequality did not predict neoliberalism at time t (φ3i) when we adjusted for the time-varying effects of HDI and Gini.



Estimates and 95% Credible Intervals (CrIs) for Model 1.





Estimates and 95% Credible Intervals (CrIs) for Model 2.





Standardized coefficients for autoregressive and cross-lagged effects in the primary model.

title: Dynamic Analysis of Economic Policies and Attitudes toward Income Inequality
text:
Takeaways


Data from more than 160 countries collected in the past 2 decades suggest that neoliberal systems have been instrumental in promoting preferences for income inequality
More generally, this work provides evidence that people’s beliefs about inequality are influenced by socioeconomic institutions and policies.

title: Gender Stereotypes and Sexist Attitudes around the World
text:
NoteAt a glance





Question

What is the relationship between stereotypes about the unique qualities that women and men possess and sexist attitudes?

Methods

Two multi-national survey studies with piecewise (spline) mixed-effects regression analysis

Finding

Overall, women are viewed as more communal and men as more agentic. These stereotypes were related to sexism: People who viewed women as more communal than men scored lower on several measures of sexism, while those who viewed men as more communal than women scored generally higher on measures of sexism (e.g., belief that men are superior, paternalism).

title: Gender Stereotypes and Sexist Attitudes around the World
text:
Background
Being communal (e.g., warm, moral, and kind) and being agentic (independent, competitive, assertive) are two sets of qualities that people use to describe themselves and others. Women are often seen as communal (and not agentic), while men are viewed as agentic (and not communal). These beliefs are called communal and agentic gender stereotypes, respectively. Theories in psychology of gender predict that stereotypes and sexist attitudes are linked. Nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this prediction is lacking. Using two multi-national datasets, we studied how endorsement of communal and agentic stereotypes promote different forms of egalitarian and sexist beliefs.

title: Gender Stereotypes and Sexist Attitudes around the World
text:
Study 1

Data

Survey data: from 14 countries, N = 7,001, with representative samples



Measures

Stereotypes: communal traits (e.g., compassionate, helpful) and agentic traits (e.g., ambitious, decisive), were rated as either “more true of women than men,” “equally true of men and women,” or “more true of men than women”. The ratings were averaged to get a composite score from -1 (more true of women than men) to 1 (more true of men than women) for communal and agentic traits.
Sexist Attitudes Outcomes: scales measuring men’s supremacy, denial of sexism, reverse sexism, traditional domestic roles
Controls: gender, subjective socioeconomic status, age



Model
We fit a mixed-effects regression predicting each outcome from communal and agentic trait ratings, with random intercept for countries. Trait ratings (i.e., communal and agentic stereotypes) are entered as splines with a knot at 0, so the slope can differ depending on whether women vs. men are seen as having more of the trait.


Show Stata code

* Splines with a knot at "equal" (0)
mkspline s1_communal 0 s2_communal = communal
mkspline s1_agentic  0 s2_agentic  = agentic

* Example outcome: men's supremacy
mixed oldf_atw s1_communal s2_communal s1_agentic s2_agentic ///
      female c_ses10 c_age || country:, reml dfmethod(kroger)

* Predicted values at women more (-1), equal (0), men more (1)
margins, at(s1_communal=-1 s2_communal=0) ///
         at(s1_communal=0  s2_communal=0) ///
         at(s1_communal=0  s2_communal=1) saving(s1_margins_ms_com, replace)

margins, at(s1_agentic=-1 s2_agentic=0) ///
         at(s1_agentic=0  s2_agentic=0) ///
         at(s1_agentic=0  s2_agentic=1) saving(s1_margins_ms_agent, replace)
The same model is fit for each of the outcomes.



Results






Figure 1: Communal stereotypes. Predicted attitudes (black line, 95% CI) by whether women or men are seen as more communal, over raw responses.









Figure 2: Agentic stereotypes. Predicted attitudes (black line, 95% CI) by whether women or men are seen as more agentic, over raw responses.



The figures are drawn in R from the margins saved in Stata:


Show R code

library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(patchwork)

df <- read_dta("data1.dta")
x_labels <- c("-1" = "-1\nWomen", "0" = "0\nEqual", "1" = "1\nMen")

# Jitter raw points to avoid overplotting
df$communal_jitter <- pmin(pmax(df$communal + runif(nrow(df), -0.4, 0.4), -1), 1)

# Predicted margins saved by Stata
df1 <- read_dta("s1_margins_ms_com.dta") %>% mutate(communal = c(-1, 0, 1))

ms_com <- ggplot(df1, aes(x = communal, y = `_margin`)) +
  geom_jitter(data = df, aes(x = communal_jitter, y = oldf_atw),
              alpha = 0.2, size = .8, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `_ci_lb`, ymax = `_ci_ub`), fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(color = "black", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-1, 0, 1), labels = x_labels) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Men's Supremacy") +
  theme_minimal()

# ...repeated for each outcome, then combined with patchwork:
combined_plot <- ((ms_com | ds_com) / (rs_com | tgr_com) / (sj_com | plot_spacer())) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

title: Gender Stereotypes and Sexist Attitudes around the World
text:
Study 2

Data

survey data from 62 countries, N = 33,313



Measures

Stereotypes: communal traits and agentic traits, were rated from 1 “more true of women than men” to 7 “more true of men than women”. These ratings were averaged to get a composite score from 1 (more true of women than men) to 7 (more true of men than women).
Sexist attitudes: scales measuring hostile views of women, benevolent sexism (e.g., paternalism), denial of sexism.
Controls: gender, subjective socioeconomic status, age



Results






Figure 3: Predicted hostile sexism, benevolent sexism, and denial of sexism by communal (left, blue) and agentic (right, red) stereotypes (95% CI).









Figure 4: Interaction of communal and agentic stereotypes. Lines show predicted values when women (blue), neither (black), or men (red) are seen as more communal, across levels of agentic stereotypes. HS = hostile sexism, BS = benevolent sexism, DS = denial of sexism.

title: Gender Stereotypes and Sexist Attitudes around the World
text:
Takeaways


Sexist attitudes were generally lowest among people who saw women as more communal.
Seeing men as more communal (and women as more agentic) was linked to stronger sexist beliefs in Study 1.
In Study 2, sexism was generally the highest among those who viewed men and women as equally communal and agentic. There was also an interaction effect such that overall assigning communality to women and agency to men was related to lower sexism.
The findings are surprising because communal stereotypes are theorized to promote sexism. By challenging previous theories, findings provide a nuanced understanding of lay beliefs about gender.
